b: p
It was a little chilly the morning of November 17 near Racine, Wisconsin. The wind was blowing hard off Lake Michigan on that bright, sunny day with temperatures in the 40s.
p
David Yamada walked along casting from a concrete lake wall. It’s a breakwall near where the Root River flows into the huge Great Lake.
p

“No one else was around fishing that morning, which I took as a bad sign,” Yamada tells Wired2fish. “I was really after steelhead and salmon. But I knew some big brown trout had been caught by some other anglers. It’s been a good year for heavyweight browns when they move near lake feeder rivers for spawning.”
p

Yamada was using spinning tackle with 24-pound test braided line and a 15-pound test fluorocarbon leader. He was casting a Berkley Unlock 72 half-ounce lure in clown color. The sinking crankbait dives and suspends and is a proven plug for a wide variety of species.
p

“I didn’t have a lot of expectations that day, and I was just casting straight out into the lake and retrieving,” said Yamada, age 58, who’d driven north to the area from his home in Vernon Hills, Illinois. “I fish there a lot, catching salmon and steelhead. It was the first time I’d used that lure.”
p
Following one cast out into the lake, Yamada felt a strike, and a heavy fish was on.
p
He battled the fish deep for a time, as it never jumped.
p

“When I saw the size of the brown trout that I’d hooked I thought there was no way I could land it,” explained Yamada, who works as an engineering consultant. “The lake waves were crashing against the breakwall, which is 8 feet above the water surface. I fought it for a while, and when it started to tire, I used my long-handled net to try and reach it.
p
“Incredibly, the lake waves just sort of surfed the fish right into my net and I got it.”
p
Yamada was able to reach his phone and record a short video of the brown trout rolling toward him in the lake’s bumpy waves.
p
“I just got the fish up onto the breakwall and unhooked it,” he said. “Then I took one photo of me holding the fish, and released it back into the lake.”
p
Yamada measured the fish’s length against his rod, then later put a tape on his measured spot.
p
“The trout was 32.5 inches long,” he said. “I didn’t get a girth of the fish. But I’ve caught salmon to 18 pounds, and that brown trout was heavier than any salmon I’ve caught.”
p
Spawning brown trout ripe with roe are at their heaviest of the year, and some length to weight charts state that a 32.5-inch brown trout can weigh 18 pounds or more.
p
“I’m just glad I got to see and catch that beautiful brown, then release it so it can spawn,” said Yamada. “Hopefully someone else can catch it in the future.”
